subject: Space exploration
title: Mars rovers
intro: Robotic rovers have driven across the surface of Mars to study its rocks, soil, and landscape.

facts.text: A radio message between Earth and Mars takes several minutes to travel, so engineers cannot steer a rover with a joystick.
facts.ev: Radio messages between Earth and Mars take several minutes to travel, so engineers cannot steer a rover with a joystick.

facts.text: Rovers receive a list of instructions from Earth and then carry out the steps on their own, often during the Martian day.
facts.ev: Rovers receive a list of instructions from Earth and then carry out the steps on their own.

facts.text: Some rovers carry drills and cameras, which allow scientists to study rocks in detail from far away.
facts.ev: Some rovers carry drills and cameras that allow scientists to study rocks in detail from far away.

facts.text: The rover Curiosity landed on Mars in 2012 inside a huge basin called Gale Crater.
facts.ev: The rover Curiosity landed on Mars in 2012 inside a huge basin called Gale Crater.

facts.text: Rover wheels are made of metal and have grooves that help them grip loose sand and rocks.
facts.ev: Rover wheels are made of metal and have grooves that help them grip loose sand and rocks.

facts.text: A day on Mars lasts about 24 hours and 37 minutes, slightly longer than a day on Earth.
facts.ev: A day on Mars lasts about 24 hours and 37 minutes, slightly longer than a day on Earth.
facts.tag: the length of a Martian day

facts.text: In 2021, a small helicopter named Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet.
facts.ev: In 2021, a small helicopter named Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet.

facts.text: Some rovers take pictures of the sky to measure how much dust is in the air.
facts.ev: Some rovers take pictures of the sky to measure how much dust is in the air.

models.q: Why do Mars rovers need to carry out instructions on their own?
models.restate: Mars rovers need to carry out instructions on their own instead of being steered directly.
models.answer: Rovers act on their own because messages from Earth arrive too slowly for real-time control.
exp: A joystick only works if the rover responds right away, which cannot happen when every signal needs minutes to cross space.
Receiving a full list in advance means the rover can keep working even while it waits for the next message.
rep: Radio messages need several minutes to travel between Earth and Mars.
Rovers get a list of instructions from Earth and then carry out the steps on their own.
models.sum: The slow trip of radio messages is why rovers must follow instructions independently.
models.sumNew: The slow trip of radio messages is why rovers work independently, and their metal wheels have grooves for gripping loose sand.
models.bad: Rovers act on their own because their batteries cannot power a radio receiver.
models.badRestate: Rovers are built with special wheels to travel across the rough Martian ground.
models.offExp: Grooved metal wheels allow a rover to keep moving across loose ground without slipping much.

models.q: How do rovers help scientists learn about Mars?
models.restate: Rovers contribute to what scientists have learned about Mars.
models.answer: Rovers help scientists by carrying instruments to places people cannot yet visit and gathering detailed observations.
exp: Examining rocks through a rover's drills and cameras lets scientists study the planet closely while staying on Earth.
Measuring dust in the air gives scientists information about the Martian atmosphere that no one on Earth could collect directly.
rep: Some rovers have drills and cameras for studying rocks from far away.
Certain rovers photograph the sky to find out how much dust is in the air.
models.sum: Rovers act as the scientists' eyes and tools on Mars, collecting data about both the ground and the sky.
models.sumNew: Rovers act as the scientists' tools on Mars, and in 2021 a helicopter named Ingenuity flew there for the first time.
models.bad: Rovers help scientists by bringing Martian rocks back to Earth so they can be tested in laboratories.
models.badRestate: A small helicopter made the first powered flight on another planet in 2021.
models.offExp: A powered flight above the surface showed that flying machines could operate on another planet.

subject: Inventions
title: The printing press
intro: Before the 1400s, books in Europe were copied by hand, a slow process that made each book rare and costly.

facts.text: Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg developed a printing system in Germany that used movable metal letters.
facts.ev: Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg developed a printing system in Germany that used movable metal letters.

facts.text: Each metal letter could be arranged into words, locked in a frame, and then reused for a different page.
facts.ev: Each metal letter could be arranged into words, locked in a frame, and then reused for a different page.

facts.text: A printer could produce hundreds of identical copies of a page using the same arranged letters.
facts.ev: A printer could produce hundreds of identical copies of a page from one arrangement of letters.

facts.text: Within about fifty years, printing shops had opened in many cities across Europe.
facts.ev: Within about fifty years, printing shops had opened in many cities across Europe.

facts.text: Printed books cost less than hand-copied ones, so more people could afford them.
facts.ev: The reading notes that printed books cost less than hand-copied ones, so more people could afford them.

facts.text: Gutenberg's press was adapted from the screw presses already used to squeeze grapes and olives.
facts.ev: Gutenberg's press was adapted from screw presses already used to squeeze grapes and olives.

facts.text: Printing ink was thick and oily so that it would stick to the metal letters.
facts.ev: Printing ink was thick and oily so that it would stick to the metal letters.

facts.text: Early printed books often copied the style of handwritten pages.
facts.ev: Early printed books often copied the style of handwritten pages.

models.q: How did movable metal letters make printing faster?
models.restate: Movable metal letters changed how quickly books could be made.
models.answer: Movable letters sped up printing because they could be reused and could produce many copies at once.
exp: Since the same letters could be rearranged for the next page, printers did not have to make a new set each time.
Making copies from one arrangement meant a page did not have to be written out again for every reader.
rep: Metal letters could be arranged into words, locked in a frame, and reused on another page.
One arrangement of letters could produce hundreds of identical page copies.
models.sum: Reusable letters and repeatable copies let printers make books much faster than hand copying.
models.sumNew: Reusable letters let printers work faster, and a thick, oily ink was used so it would stick to the metal.
models.bad: Movable letters sped up printing because they wrote the words on their own without any human help.
models.badRestate: The ink used in printing needed to stick well to metal letters.
models.offExp: A sticky ink was needed so that the letters would leave a clear mark on the paper.

models.q: Why did the printing press lead to more people owning books?
models.restate: The printing press made it possible for many more people to own books.
models.answer: The press led to wider book ownership because it lowered prices and let printing spread quickly to new places.
exp: When a book costs less, families with modest incomes can buy one instead of leaving books to the wealthy few.
As printing shops opened in more cities, books could be made close to the readers who wanted them.
rep: Printed books cost less than hand-copied books, so more people could buy them.
Printing shops had opened in many European cities within about fifty years.
models.sum: Overall, cheaper books and a growing number of printing shops put books within reach of many more people.
models.sumNew: Overall, cheaper books and more printing shops put books within reach of many people, and Gutenberg adapted his press from screw presses used for grapes.
models.bad: The press led to wider ownership because every printed book was given away for free.
models.badRestate: Gutenberg's press borrowed ideas from machines that were already used on farms.
models.offExp: Reusing an existing machine design helped Gutenberg build his press without inventing every part from scratch.

subject: Environmental science
title: Coral reefs
intro: A coral reef is a structure in warm, shallow ocean water built by tiny animals called corals.

facts.text: Reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet about a quarter of all ocean species depend on them at some point.
facts.ev: Reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet about a quarter of all ocean species depend on them at some point.

facts.text: Many young fish live among the branches of coral until they are large enough to survive in open water.
facts.ev: Many young fish live among the branches of coral until they are large enough to survive in open water.

facts.text: A reef forms a barrier that breaks up waves before they reach the shore.
facts.ev: A reef forms a barrier that breaks up waves before they reach the shore.

facts.text: Corals build hard skeletons of limestone, and over many years the skeletons pile up to form the reef.
facts.ev: Corals build hard skeletons of limestone, and over many years the skeletons pile up to form the reef.

facts.text: Tiny algae live inside coral and make food from sunlight, which is why reefs grow in shallow, sunny water.
facts.ev: Tiny algae live inside coral and make food from sunlight, which is why reefs grow in shallow, sunny water.

facts.text: Many reefs attract visitors who enjoy swimming and snorkeling.
facts.ev: Many reefs attract visitors who enjoy swimming and snorkeling.

facts.text: The largest reef system, the Great Barrier Reef near Australia, can be seen from space.
facts.ev: The largest reef system, the Great Barrier Reef near Australia, can be seen from space.

facts.text: Divers sometimes find reef animals in bright colors, including blue, orange, and yellow fish.
facts.ev: Divers sometimes find reef animals in bright colors, including blue, orange, and yellow fish.

models.q: Why are coral reefs important to ocean life?
models.restate: Coral reefs matter a great deal to the life of the ocean.
models.answer: Coral reefs are important because they provide homes and shelter for a large share of ocean animals.
exp: A tiny fraction of the sea floor supporting so many species means that damage to a reef would affect a great deal of ocean life.
Shelter among the coral protects young fish while they grow, so more of them can reach adulthood.
rep: Reefs cover under one percent of the ocean floor, but about a quarter of ocean species rely on them.
Young fish often live in the branches of coral until they can survive in open water.
models.sum: Reefs deserve attention because so many ocean animals depend on them for shelter and growth.
models.sumNew: Reefs deserve attention because so many animals depend on them, and many reefs attract visitors who enjoy snorkeling.
models.bad: Coral reefs are important because they produce most of the oxygen in the atmosphere.
models.badRestate: Many people travel to reefs to enjoy swimming and snorkeling.
models.offExp: Visitors who snorkel above a reef can see the wildlife without having to dive deep.

models.q: How does a coral reef come to protect a nearby shore?
models.restate: The way a coral reef comes to protect a nearby shore can be explained.
models.answer: A reef protects the shore because corals build a solid barrier that weakens approaching waves.
exp: Because the skeletons pile up over many years, the reef grows into a large, solid structure rather than a thin layer.
Waves that lose energy against the reef arrive at the beach with less force than they began with.
rep: Limestone skeletons built by corals pile up over many years to form a reef.
A reef acts as a barrier that breaks up waves before they reach land.
models.sum: By growing into a barrier that takes the force out of waves, a reef shields the shore.
models.sumNew: By growing into a barrier, a reef shields the shore, and tiny algae inside the corals make food from sunlight.
models.bad: A reef protects the shore because its bright colors scare large waves away.
models.badRestate: Corals grow in sunny water because algae living inside them need light.
models.offExp: Since the algae make food from sunlight, coral can grow well only where light reaches it.

subject: Weather and climate
title: Lightning and thunder
intro: Lightning is a giant spark of electricity that jumps through the air during some storms.

facts.text: Inside a storm cloud, ice crystals and water droplets collide, and these collisions separate electric charges within the cloud.
facts.ev: Inside a storm cloud, colliding ice crystals and water droplets separate electric charges.

facts.text: When the difference in electric charge becomes large enough, a spark leaps between the cloud and the ground or between parts of the cloud.
facts.ev: When the difference in electric charge becomes large enough, a spark leaps between the cloud and the ground or within the cloud.

facts.text: A lightning bolt heats the air around it to about 30,000 degrees Celsius, far hotter than the surface of the Sun.
facts.ev: A lightning bolt heats the surrounding air to about 30,000 degrees Celsius, far hotter than the surface of the Sun.
facts.tag: the extreme heat of a bolt

facts.text: The heated air expands so quickly that it creates a booming sound wave, which people hear as thunder.
facts.ev: The heated air expands so quickly that it creates a booming sound wave that people hear as thunder.

facts.text: Light travels much faster than sound, so people see a flash before they hear thunder.
facts.ev: The passage explains that light travels much faster than sound, so people see a flash before they hear thunder.

facts.text: Counting the seconds between a flash and its thunder can tell a person roughly how far away the strike was.
facts.ev: Counting the seconds between a flash and its thunder can tell a person roughly how far away the strike was.

facts.text: Tall, pointed objects such as trees and towers are more likely to be struck.
facts.ev: Tall, pointed objects such as trees and towers are more likely to be struck.

facts.text: Lightning rods are metal poles that give a strike a safe path to the ground.
facts.ev: Lightning rods are metal poles that give a strike a safe path to the ground.

models.q: What causes the sound of thunder?
models.restate: The sound of thunder has a cause that can be explained.
models.answer: Thunder is caused by air that lightning heats so fast that it expands violently.
exp: Such an enormous jump in temperature gives the surrounding air no time to adjust gradually.
The sudden expansion pushes air outward in a wave, and that moving wave is what reaches our ears as a boom.
rep: A lightning bolt heats the air around it to about 30,000 degrees Celsius.
Heated air expands quickly and makes a sound wave that people hear as thunder.
models.sum: In short, thunder is the sound of air that was heated and pushed outward by a lightning bolt.
models.sumNew: In short, thunder is the sound of air pushed outward by a bolt, and metal lightning rods guide strikes safely to the ground.
models.bad: Thunder is caused by storm clouds crashing into each other like heavy objects.
models.badRestate: Lightning rods are used on buildings to guide strikes toward the ground.
models.offExp: A metal pole offers a path that carries the electricity safely away from a building.

models.q: How can a person estimate how far away a lightning strike was?
models.restate: There is a way for a person to estimate how far away a lightning strike was.
models.answer: A person can estimate the distance by timing the gap between the flash and the thunder.
exp: Because light arrives almost instantly, the flash marks the moment of the strike, and the thunder follows later.
A longer count means the sound had farther to travel, so the strike must have been farther away.
rep: Light travels much faster than sound, so a flash is seen before thunder is heard.
Counting the seconds between a flash and thunder gives a rough idea of the distance.
models.sum: The delay between flash and thunder gives people a simple way to judge how far away a strike was.
models.sumNew: The delay between flash and thunder shows how far away a strike was, and tall, pointed objects are more likely to be hit.
models.bad: A person can estimate the distance by measuring how bright the flash looks at night.
models.badRestate: Tall, pointed objects such as trees and towers are struck more often than shorter objects.
models.offExp: Since tall, pointed objects stand above their surroundings, a bolt is more likely to reach them first.

subject: Computer technology
title: Binary numbers
intro: Computers store and process all information, from photos to music, using only two symbols: 0 and 1.

facts.text: Each 0 or 1 is called a bit, and a bit can be represented by a switch that is either off or on.
facts.ev: Each 0 or 1 is called a bit, and a bit can be represented by a switch that is either off or on.

facts.text: Eight bits grouped together make one byte, which can form 256 different patterns.
facts.ev: Eight bits grouped together make one byte, which can form 256 different patterns.

facts.text: Each letter and symbol on a keyboard is assigned its own number, which is stored as a pattern of bits.
facts.ev: The source states that each letter and symbol on a keyboard is assigned its own number, which is stored as a pattern of bits.

facts.text: In binary counting, each place is worth twice as much as the place to its right, such as 1, 2, 4, and 8.
facts.ev: In binary counting, each place is worth twice as much as the place to its right, such as 1, 2, 4, and 8.

facts.text: Electronic circuits can tell two states apart very reliably, such as high voltage and low voltage.
facts.ev: Electronic circuits can tell two states apart very reliably, such as high voltage and low voltage.

facts.text: A kilobyte is about one thousand bytes, and a short email might take up a few kilobytes.
facts.ev: A kilobyte is about one thousand bytes, and a short email might take up a few kilobytes.

facts.text: Early computers filled whole rooms and were operated using punched cards.
facts.ev: Early computers filled whole rooms and were operated using punched cards.

facts.text: Colors on a screen are stored as numbers that tell how much red, green, and blue light to show.
facts.ev: Colors on a screen are stored as numbers that tell how much red, green, and blue light to show.

models.q: Why do computers use only two symbols to store information?
models.restate: Computers rely on just two symbols to represent every kind of information.
models.answer: Computers use two symbols because circuits can reliably tell two states apart and group them into larger patterns.
exp: If a circuit only has to choose between two states, mistakes are less likely than if it had to tell many levels apart.
Grouping eight bits gives hundreds of patterns, so two symbols are enough to represent a great variety of things.
rep: Electronic circuits can reliably tell two states apart, such as high and low voltage.
A byte is eight bits and can form 256 different patterns.
models.sum: Two reliable symbols, grouped into patterns, give computers all they need to store information.
models.sumNew: Two reliable symbols grouped into patterns are enough for computers, and early computers were run with punched cards.
models.bad: Computers use two symbols because larger sets of symbols cannot be shown on a screen.
models.badRestate: Early computers were very large machines that were operated with punched cards.
models.offExp: Because they relied on punched cards, early computers had to be given information in a very different way.

models.q: How can a computer store written text using only numbers?
models.restate: The way a computer stores written text using only numbers can be explained.
models.answer: A computer stores text by giving each character a number and recording that number as a pattern of bits.
exp: Because every character has its own number, the computer can keep a letter by recording its number instead of its shape.
Place values let a row of 0s and 1s stand for larger numbers, so even a long list of characters can be written in two symbols.
rep: Each keyboard letter and symbol is given a number stored as a pattern of bits.
In binary counting, each place is worth twice the place to its right, such as 1, 2, 4, and 8.
models.sum: Overall, text can be stored because characters become numbers and numbers can be written as patterns of bits.
models.sumNew: Overall, text becomes numbers and then bits, and screen colors are also stored as numbers for red, green, and blue light.
models.bad: A computer stores text by taking a tiny photograph of each letter and saving the picture.
models.badRestate: A computer stores screen colors by saving how much red, green, and blue light to show.
models.offExp: Since colors are stored as numbers, the screen can recreate a color by showing the right amount of each light.
